I've been watching AI write code for two years now. And I've noticed something that nobody talks about enough: **the model is almost never the bottleneck. The context is.** Claude Opus can reason through algorithms that would take me an hour. It can refactor a 500-line function into clean, testable modules in seconds. But ask it to add a feature to a real codebase — one with 200+ files, custom conventions, internal APIs, and six months of accumulated decisions — and it sometimes struggles. Not because it's dumb (hallucinations have reduced incredibly in the last few years). Because it's blind. ## What is TaskAI? [TaskAI](https://taskai.cc) is something I've been building for the past year — an AI-native project management system designed from the ground up around one idea: **AI agents should be first-class participants in your development workflow, not afterthoughts.** It has the things you'd expect — kanban boards, sprint planning, task management. But the pieces that make it different are the ones I built specifically for AI: - **A collaborative wiki** — real-time markdown editing (powered by [Yjs](https://yjs.dev/) CRDTs) where teams document architecture decisions, API contracts, deployment guides, and the kind of tribal knowledge that usually lives in someone's head or a forgotten Slack thread. - **An [MCP](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/) server** — so AI agents like [Claude Code](https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/claude-code) can create tasks, search documentation, read wiki pages, and update project state through tool calls. Not a chat integration. Actual tool-use over a structured protocol. - **A built-in drawing canvas** — for architecture diagrams, flow charts, and system designs that live alongside the documentation, not in a separate tool. - **GitHub two-way sync** — issues and PRs flow between GitHub and TaskAI automatically, so the AI sees the full picture. I've been using it daily with Claude Code on multiple projects. And the thing I kept running into wasn't a TaskAI problem or a Claude problem — it was a *knowledge retrieval* problem. The documentation was there. The AI just couldn't find the right parts at the right time. That's the story behind what I'm calling the **Knowledge Spine**, and why I think it matters more than any model upgrade. ## The Needle Nobody Can Find Here's a scenario every developer using AI has experienced. You're working on a Go backend. You ask Claude to "add rate limiting to the login endpoint." The model generates clean, functional code. It uses the `golang.org/x/time/rate` package, creates a middleware, applies it to the route. One problem: your project already has a rate limiter. It lives in `internal/middleware/ratelimit.go`. It uses a custom token bucket backed by Redis. It has tests. It follows your team's error response format. The AI didn't know any of this. This isn't a context window problem. Your codebase might fit comfortably within [Claude's 1M token window](https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/about-claude/models). But dumping a million tokens into a prompt is like giving someone a library card and asking them to write a book report in 30 seconds. The information is *there*. It's just not *findable*. Greg Kamradt's [Needle in a Haystack test](https://github.com/gkamradt/LLMTest_NeedleInAHaystack) proved this empirically. Even models that claim 200K+ context degrade badly when the relevant information sits in the middle of a long input. The "lost in the middle" phenomenon is real, it's measured, and it gets worse as context grows.[^1] ## What Actually Determines Code Quality After months of using Claude Code on the [TaskAI](https://taskai.cc) codebase daily, I noticed a pattern: **The quality of AI-generated code is almost entirely determined by the quality of context it receives.** Not the model size. Not the temperature. Not the system prompt. The context. When I manually paste the right files into the conversation — the handler I'm extending, the middleware it depends on, the test patterns we use — the output is indistinguishable from what I'd write myself. When I don't, it's a coin flip. This is what I call the **Knowledge Spine** problem. Every codebase has one — a structural backbone of conventions, patterns, APIs, and decisions that make code "fit." Humans absorb it over weeks of onboarding. AI needs it served on a platter, in exactly the right moment, for exactly the right query.
## The Approach Everyone Tries (And Why It Fails) The obvious solution is to stuff more code into the context window. [Cursor](https://cursor.com/) does this by indexing your workspace. [Sourcegraph Cody](https://sourcegraph.com/cody) embeds entire repositories. [Augment Code](https://www.augmentcode.com/) reports processing 400K+ files through semantic dependency analysis.[^2] These are all doing the right thing. But they're doing it at the wrong layer. Think about how *you* work on a large codebase. You don't re-read the entire repo every time you make a change. You have a mental model — built from architecture docs, team wikis, PR review comments, and that one Slack message from three months ago where someone explained why the auth middleware works the way it does. That mental model is your personal Knowledge Spine. Developer tools are trying to build this from code alone. Parse the AST, follow imports, rank by file proximity. It works for small projects. It fails spectacularly on anything with real architecture, because architecture decisions aren't *in* the code. They're in the heads of the people who wrote it. Or, if you're lucky, in documentation. ## Building a Knowledge Spine (Not a Bigger Brain) Here's what I did instead. TaskAI's wiki already had sixty-five pages of accumulated project knowledge — architecture decisions, API contracts, deployment pipelines, design rationale. The stuff that normally lives in Notion, Confluence, or someone's memory. And the MCP server already had a `search_wiki` tool so AI agents could search it. But the search was `ILIKE` — PostgreSQL's case-insensitive substring matching. No ranking, no semantic understanding. Searching "how does deployment work" returned nothing because no wiki page contains that literal string. So I built a Knowledge Spine. Three components, all running on a single server, all local, zero external API calls: **1. [Ollama](https://ollama.com/) sidecar** — A tiny embedding model ([all-MiniLM-L6-v2](https://huggingface.co/sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2), 45MB) running as a Docker container. It converts text into 384-dimensional vectors. No GPU needed. About 150MB of RAM and 10 milliseconds per embedding. **2. [pgvector](https://github.com/pgvector/pgvector)** — PostgreSQL extension for vector similarity search. An [HNSW index](https://arxiv.org/abs/1603.09320) on the embedding column gives us approximate nearest-neighbor search in sub-millisecond time. **3. The embedding pipeline** — Every two minutes, a background worker scans for updated wiki pages, splits them into blocks by heading, and embeds each block. When an AI agent searches, the query gets embedded the same way, and cosine similarity finds the most relevant blocks — regardless of wording.
The entire system cost me about a day to build. The [migration](https://github.com/biswas-dev/taskai) is 6 lines of SQL. The embedding client is 130 lines of Go. The search handler supports four modes — keyword, full-text, semantic, and hybrid — selectable via a single `mode` parameter on the MCP tool. ## Why Hybrid Search Changes Everything Here's the thing about vector search that most articles get wrong: semantic search alone isn't enough. If you search "OAuth2" and the document says "OAuth2", you want an exact match, not a semantic approximation. But if you search "how do we handle user login" and the document is titled "Authentication & Authorization Flow", you need semantic understanding. The answer is hybrid search. We run both full-text (PostgreSQL's built-in [tsvector](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/textsearch.html) with GIN indexing) and vector search in parallel, then merge the results using [Reciprocal Rank Fusion](https://plg.uwaterloo.ca/~gvcormac/cormacksigir09-rrf.pdf).[^3] RRF is elegant because it works on *rank positions*, not raw scores. No normalization needed. A document ranked #1 by both systems gets a higher fused score than one ranked #1 by one system and #50 by the other. The formula is simple: ``` score(doc) = 1/(60 + fts_rank) + 1/(60 + vector_rank) ``` This is the same approach used by [Elasticsearch](https://www.elastic.co/guide/en/elasticsearch/reference/current/rrf.html), [Weaviate](https://weaviate.io/), and [Vespa](https://vespa.ai/) in their hybrid search implementations. It works remarkably well.
## The MCP Connection All of this is exposed through [Model Context Protocol](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/) — Anthropic's open standard for connecting AI applications to external tools and data.[^4] When Claude Code is connected to TaskAI's MCP server, it gets a single tool: `search_wiki`. One parameter for the query, one for the search mode. The AI doesn't know it's querying a vector database. It doesn't need to. It asks "how does the deployment pipeline work?" and gets back the three most relevant wiki sections, ranked by semantic relevance, in under 50 milliseconds. Then it writes code that actually follows your deployment patterns. This is why I care about [MCP](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/) more than I care about model improvements. A smarter model with bad context produces bad code confidently. A decent model with great context produces code that fits your codebase like it was written by someone who's been on the team for six months. ## What I Learned from MemPalace I want to credit [MemPalace](https://github.com/mempalace/mempalace), an open-source local-first AI memory system, for several ideas that influenced this design.[^5] Their hierarchical scoping concept — organizing memory into Wings, Rooms, and Drawers instead of flat-searching an entire corpus — directly inspired our project-scoped search. An AI agent searching the TaskAI wiki only sees pages from projects they have access to, not the entire knowledge base. Their commitment to verbatim preservation (storing original content, not lossy summaries) validated our approach of embedding full text blocks rather than generated summaries. And their zero-API-dependency architecture (96.6% recall@5 on the LongMemEval benchmark, entirely local) pushed us toward [Ollama](https://ollama.com/) instead of calling OpenAI's embedding API. Everything runs on a single AMD EPYC server. No API keys. No network dependency. No usage bills. Where we diverge: MemPalace is designed for conversation memory. Our Knowledge Spine is designed for structured project knowledge — architecture docs, API references, deployment guides. Different problem, same principle. ## The Real Numbers Here's what's running in production right now on [taskai.cc](https://taskai.cc): | Component | Detail | |-----------|--------| | Wiki pages | 65 | | Indexed blocks | 1,052 | | Embedded blocks | 1,034 (98.3%) | | Embedding model | all-MiniLM-L6-v2 (384 dim) | | Model size | 45MB on disk | | Ollama RAM | ~150MB | | Embedding latency | ~10ms per block | | Search latency | <50ms end-to-end | | Server | Single AMD EPYC, 31GB RAM | | Infrastructure cost | $0 additional (runs on existing server) | The Ollama container uses 0.5% of the server's available RAM. The [pgvector](https://github.com/pgvector/pgvector) HNSW index adds negligible storage. The embedding pipeline runs in the background every two minutes and is invisible to users. ## Why This Matters Beyond Opus 4.7 Models will keep getting smarter. [Context windows](https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/about-claude/models) will keep growing. But the fundamental problem doesn't change: an LLM can only write good code if it understands the *context* that code lives in. A 10M token context window doesn't solve this. You can't index a large codebase by dumping it all into a prompt, and even if you could, the "lost in the middle" problem means the model would still miss the relevant parts. What you need is a system that understands *what's relevant to the current question* and retrieves exactly that. That's what a Knowledge Spine does. It's not a replacement for bigger models or longer contexts. It's the layer that makes them actually useful. The knowledge management market is projected to reach [$32 billion by 2030](https://ttms.com/10-best-ai-tools-for-knowledge-management-in-large-enterprises-2025/), driven largely by AI integration.[^6] But most of that is about *human* knowledge management. What I'm arguing is that the same infrastructure — wikis, documentation, structured knowledge — is now AI infrastructure too. Your knowledge base is no longer "nice to have" documentation. It's the difference between an AI that writes broken code and one that writes production-quality code. Every wiki page you maintain, every architecture decision you document, every API contract you write down — it's all training data for the next time an AI agent touches your codebase. ## Try It Yourself [TaskAI](https://taskai.cc) is live. The MCP server is at `mcp.taskai.cc`. Connect Claude Code, ask it to search your project wiki, and watch what happens when the AI actually *knows* your codebase. The Knowledge Spine is open and inspectable — you can see the [source code](https://github.com/biswas-dev/taskai), the [migration](https://github.com/biswas-dev/taskai), and the [embedding client](https://github.com/biswas-dev/taskai). The entire vector search implementation is about 500 lines of Go. Because the next frontier of AI-assisted development isn't smarter models. It's smarter context. --- *This is Part 1 of a series on building AI-native development tools. Next: how to build feedback loops that let LLMs improve their own Knowledge Spine over time.* [^1]: Liu et al. — [Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.03172) (2023). Demonstrated that LLM performance degrades significantly when relevant information is in the middle of the input, even when the context window technically supports the length. [^2]: Augment Code — [Context Engine Architecture](https://www.augmentcode.com/) (2025). Reports 70.6% on SWE-bench vs GitHub Copilot's 54%, attributing the gap primarily to context quality rather than model capability. [^3]: Cormack, Clarke & Buettcher — [Reciprocal Rank Fusion outperforms Condorcet and individual rank learning methods](https://plg.uwaterloo.ca/~gvcormac/cormacksigir09-rrf.pdf) (SIGIR 2009). The foundational paper on RRF, showing that simple rank-based fusion consistently outperforms more sophisticated methods. [^4]: Anthropic — [Introducing the Model Context Protocol](https://www.anthropic.com/news/model-context-protocol) (2024). The open standard for connecting AI applications to external tools and data sources, now maintained by the Linux Foundation. [^5]: MemPalace — [Local-first AI memory system](https://github.com/mempalace/mempalace) (2025). Achieves 96.6% recall@5 on LongMemEval entirely locally. Hierarchical scoping (Wings/Rooms/Drawers) and verbatim preservation are key design principles. [^6]: TTMS — [AI Tools for Knowledge Management](https://ttms.com/10-best-ai-tools-for-knowledge-management-in-large-enterprises-2025/) (2025). Knowledge management software market valued at $13.70B in 2025, projected to reach $32.15B by 2030 (18.6% CAGR).

Handles go-draw diagrams (create, populate, embed), footnote references, post CRUD via API, cover image upload, and content formatting. Use when the user says "blog", "create a post", "edit post", "add diagram", "add reference", "go-draw", "new drawing", or "/blog". user_invocable: true --- # Blog Management — anshumanbiswas.com Create, edit, and enhance blog posts on the Go-based blog at anshumanbiswas.com. ## Authentication API token (works for all endpoints including file uploads): ``` TOKEN="REDACTED" ``` All API calls use: `Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN` and `User-Agent: Mozilla/5.0` (required — Cloudflare blocks default user agents). ## Available Categories | ID | Name | |----|------| | 5 | AI | | 9 | AIAgentLens | | 2 | Architecture | | 4 | Cloud Computing | | 6 | Security | | 8 | SaaS | | 3 | Performance | Posts tagged `AIAgentLens` (ID 9) auto-sync to aiagentlens.com/blog within 24h. --- ## Complete Blog Post Creation Workflow This is the end-to-end workflow for creating a blog post with diagrams, cover image, and references: ### Step 1: Research the topic Use WebSearch/WebFetch to gather source material. Save key facts for the post. ### Step 2: Create go-draw diagrams Create diagrams BEFORE writing the post so you have the embed IDs ready. ### Step 3: Write the post content Save to `/tmp/post_content.md`. Include: - `` read-more break after the intro paragraph - Go-draw embeds where diagrams should appear - Footnote references `[^N]` inline + `[^N]:` definitions at bottom - Natural, human writing style ### Step 4: Create the post via API ```python python3 << 'PYEOF' import json, urllib.request TOKEN = "REDACTED" with open('/tmp/post_content.md') as f: content = f.read() payload = { "UserID": 1, "CategoryID": 1, "Title": "Post Title Here", "Content": content, "Slug": "post-slug-here", "IsPublished": False, "Featured": True, "FeaturedImageURL": "" } data = json.dumps(payload).encode() req = urllib.request.Request( "https://anshumanbiswas.com/api/posts", data=data, headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {TOKEN}", "Content-Type": "application/json", "User-Agent": "Mozilla/5.0"}, method="POST", ) with urllib.request.urlopen(req) as r: resp = json.loads(r.read()) print("Post ID:", resp.get("ID")) PYEOF ``` **IMPORTANT**: Create endpoint uses **PascalCase** field names: `UserID`, `CategoryID`, `Title`, `Content`, `Slug`, `IsPublished`, `Featured`, `FeaturedImageURL`. ### Step 5: Upload cover image The upload endpoint accepts Bearer token auth. Supports: jpg, png, gif, webp, svg, pdf. ```bash curl -s -X POST \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \ -A "Mozilla/5.0" \ -F "file=@/tmp/cover.svg" \ "https://anshumanbiswas.com/admin/uploads?type=featured&slug=post-slug-here" ``` Returns: `{"url": "/static/uploads/featured/post-slug-here/abc123.svg"}` Featured images are auto-compressed to max 600px wide at JPEG quality 80 (except SVGs). ### Step 6: Update post with cover + categories + publish ```python python3 << 'PYEOF' import json, urllib.request TOKEN = "REDACTED" with open('/tmp/post_content.md') as f: content = f.read() update = { "title": "Post Title Here", "content": content, "slug": "post-slug-here", "is_published": False, "featured": True, "featured_image_url": "/static/uploads/featured/post-slug-here/abc123.svg", "categories": [5, 9, 6] } data = json.dumps(update).encode() req = urllib.request.Request( "https://anshumanbiswas.com/api/posts/{POST_ID}", data=data, headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {TOKEN}", "Content-Type": "application/json", "User-Agent": "Mozilla/5.0"}, method="PUT", ) with urllib.request.urlopen(req) as r: print("Updated:", r.read().decode()[:100]) PYEOF ``` **IMPORTANT**: Update endpoint uses **lowercase/snake_case** field names: `title`, `content`, `slug`, `is_published`, `featured`, `featured_image_url`, `categories`. --- ## SVG Cover Images Create animated SVG covers with **transparent background** and small file size (~5KB): - **MUST be transparent** — no `` background fill. Base directory for this skill: /Users/anshumanbiswas/.claude/skills/dev-server

# Local Development Server

Start a local dev environment for any project that has a `.me.sh` adapter file.
All projects live under `~/play/` and use the unified runner at `~/play/me/scripts/server`.

## How It Works

Each project has:
- `.me.sh` — project adapter with metadata (name, ports, stack, DB type)
- `docker-compose.yml` — containerized services (postgres, redis, etc.)
- `script/server` or `scripts/server` — project-specific server management

## Steps

### 1. Detect the current project

Look for `.me.sh` in the current working directory to get project metadata:

```bash
source .me.sh  # Gets PROJECT_NAME, PROJECT_PORT_BACKEND, PROJECT_PORT_FRONTEND, PROJECT_DB, PROJECT_DOMAIN, etc.
```

### 2. Parse the user's request

The user may specify:
- **Environment to point frontend at**: `prod`, `staging`, `uat`, or `local` (default: `local`)
- **What to start**: `all` (default), `frontend`, `backend`, `docker`

### 3. Start Docker services (database)

Most projects need PostgreSQL (or SQLite). Start the database via docker-compose:

```bash
cd <project_dir>
docker compose up -d postgres  # Start just postgres (not all services)
```

Wait for postgres to be healthy before proceeding:

```bash
docker compose exec postgres pg_isready -U <user> -d <db>
```

If the project uses Redis too, also start it:

```bash
docker compose up -d postgres redis
```

### 4. Start the backend (API server)

**Only needed when pointing to `local`.** When pointing to prod/staging/uat, skip this step — the Vite proxy forwards to the remote API directly.

Run the backend natively for hot-reload. Each project's `.me.sh` defines how:

```bash
# For projects with Makefile:
cd <project_dir>/api && make dev

# Or use the adapter's local_dev function via the universal runner:
~/play/me/scripts/server local dev <project_name>
```

The backend runs on `PROJECT_PORT_BACKEND` (e.g., 8083 for TaskAI, 8080 for Pingrly).

### 5. Start the frontend with Vite proxy (CRITICAL)

**IMPORTANT: Use `VITE_PROXY_TARGET` with Vite's built-in proxy, NOT `VITE_API_URL`.**

Setting `VITE_API_URL` to a remote domain causes CORS errors because the browser sends cross-origin requests. Instead, Vite's dev server proxy handles `/api` requests server-side, forwarding them to the target — no CORS issues.

Projects with Vite have `vite.config.ts` configured to read `VITE_PROXY_TARGET`:

```typescript
// In vite.config.ts:
const proxyTarget = process.env.VITE_PROXY_TARGET || 'http://localhost:8080'
// ...
proxy: {
  '/api': { target: proxyTarget, changeOrigin: true, secure: true },
}
```

**If a project's vite.config.ts does NOT already read `VITE_PROXY_TARGET`**, add this pattern to it before starting.

Resolve the proxy target URL from the environment:

| Environment | VITE_PROXY_TARGET |
|-------------|-------------------|
| `local` | `http://localhost:<PROJECT_PORT_BACKEND>` (default, no env var needed) |
| `staging` | `https://staging.<PROJECT_DOMAIN>` |
| `uat` | `https://uat.<PROJECT_DOMAIN>` |
| `prod` | `https://<PROJECT_DOMAIN>` |

Then start:

```bash
cd <project_dir>/web
VITE_PROXY_TARGET=<url> npx vite --port <PROJECT_PORT_FRONTEND> --host
```

The browser only talks to `localhost:<PORT>` — Vite proxies `/api/*` to the target server-side.

### 6. Report status

After starting, confirm all services are running:

```bash
# Check API (through proxy)
curl -s http://localhost:<PROJECT_PORT_FRONTEND>/api/health

# Check frontend
curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}" http://localhost:<PROJECT_PORT_FRONTEND>/
```

Print the URLs:
```
Local dev server running:
  Frontend: http://localhost:<PROJECT_PORT_FRONTEND>
  API proxy: -> <VITE_PROXY_TARGET>
  Pointing to: <environment>
```

## Environment Domains by Project

These are read from `.me.sh`'s `PROJECT_DOMAIN`:

| Project | Domain | Staging | UAT |
|---------|--------|---------|-----|
| taskai | taskai.cc | staging.taskai.cc | uat.taskai.cc |
| pingrly | pingrly.com | staging.pingrly.com | uat.pingrly.com |
| blog | anshumanbiswas.com | staging.anshumanbiswas.com | - |
| folioworth | folioworth.com | staging.folioworth.com | uat.folioworth.com |
| elephanto | elephantoevents.ca | staging.elephantoevents.ca | - |
| flags | flagtgl.com | staging.flagtgl.com | - |

## Project Port Map

| Project | Backend | Frontend |
|---------|---------|----------|
| taskai | 8083 | 5174 |
| pingrly | 8080 | 3000 |
| blog | 22222 | - |
| folioworth | 8180 | 5173 |
| elephanto | 8080 | 3000 |
| flags | 8081 | 3000 |
| biswas | 9000 | 3001 |

## Important Notes

- **NEVER use `VITE_API_URL` to point to remote environments** — this causes CORS errors. Always use `VITE_PROXY_TARGET` with Vite's dev proxy instead.
- **Always start Docker postgres first** if the project uses PostgreSQL and pointing to `local`
- When pointing to prod/staging/uat, you don't need a local backend or database — the Vite proxy forwards API calls to the remote server
- OAuth login (GitHub/Google) works through the proxy since the browser sees everything as localhost
- Use `docker compose up -d postgres` (not `docker compose up`) to avoid starting ALL services
- The universal runner is at `~/play/me/scripts/server` — it discovers all projects with `.me.sh`

## Stopping

```bash
# Kill frontend dev server (find PID on the port)
lsof -ti:<PROJECT_PORT_FRONTEND> | xargs kill 2>/dev/null

# Kill backend (only if running locally)
lsof -ti:<PROJECT_PORT_BACKEND> | xargs kill 2>/dev/null

# Stop docker services
docker compose stop postgres
```

## Examples

**Start TaskAI locally pointing to production (most common):**
```bash
cd /Users/anshumanbiswas/play/taskai/web
VITE_PROXY_TARGET=https://taskai.cc npx vite --port 5174 --host
# No backend or postgres needed — proxy handles everything
```

**Start TaskAI pointing to staging:**
```bash
cd /Users/anshumanbiswas/play/taskai/web
VITE_PROXY_TARGET=https://staging.taskai.cc npx vite --port 5174 --host
```

**Start TaskAI fully local (with local backend + postgres):**
```bash
cd /Users/anshumanbiswas/play/taskai
docker compose up -d postgres       # Start database
cd api && make dev &                 # Start backend on :8083
cd ../web && npx vite --port 5174 --host  # Frontend proxies to localhost:8080 by default
```

**Start Pingrly locally pointing to production:**
```bash
cd /Users/anshumanbiswas/play/pingrly/web  # or frontend/
VITE_PROXY_TARGET=https://pingrly.com npx vite --port 3000 --host
```

**Full Docker mode (all services containerized):**
```bash
./script/server local:start  # or docker compose up -d --build
```

1 // Package blogsync pulls posts tagged with a given category from a remote 2 // anshumanbiswas.com-compatible blog API and materialises them as markdown 3 // files (YAML frontmatter + body) for the go-blog engine to serve. 4 // 5 // The sync is idempotent: files are only rewritten when the rendered bytes 6 // differ from what is already on disk. LastEditDate is written into the 7 // frontmatter, so upstream edits naturally trigger a rewrite. 8 // 9 // Go-draw embeds (
) are 10 // detected in the source content and replaced with inline tags 11 // pointing at locally-cached SVGs under /_images/. The SVGs are 12 // fetched from /draw/{id}/export.svg on each sync; writes are 13 // idempotent, so images that haven't changed upstream are a no-op. 14 // 15 // Use Run(ctx, ...) to start a scheduler that syncs immediately and then 16 // every interval thereafter. Use SyncOnce for a single pass. 17 package blogsync 18 19 import ( 20 "bytes" 21 "context" 22 "encoding/json" 23 "fmt" 24 "io" 25 "log" 26 "net/http" 27 "os" 28 "path/filepath" 29 "regexp" 30 "strings" 31 "time" 32 ) 33 34 // Config controls a sync. 35 type Config struct { 36 SourceURL string // e.g. "https://anshumanbiswas.com" 37 Tag string // filter: posts with this category (case-insensitive) 38 PostsDir string // output directory 39 UserAgent string // HTTP User-Agent (Cloudflare blocks some defaults) 40 Timeout time.Duration // per-request timeout 41 } 42 43 // Result summarises a sync pass. 44 type Result struct { 45 Fetched int // posts pulled from remote 46 Matched int // posts with the configured tag 47 Written int // markdown files created or updated 48 Unchanged int // markdown files skipped because content is identical 49 Errors int // per-post failures 50 ImagesFetched int // go-draw SVGs downloaded (new or changed)

func getEnv(key, fallback string) string {
	if v := os.Getenv(key); v != "" {

	}

[TaskAI](https://taskai.cc) is something I've been building for the past year — an AI-native project management system designed from the ground up around one idea: **AI agents should be first-class participants in your development workflow, not afterthoughts.** It has the things you'd expect — kanban boards, sprint planning, task management. Not a chat integration. Actual tool-use over a structured protocol. - **A built-in drawing canvas** — for architecture diagrams, flow charts, and system designs that live alongside the documentation, not in a separate tool. - **GitHub two-way sync** — issues and PRs flow between GitHub and TaskAI automatically, so the AI sees the full picture. I've been using it daily with Claude Code on multiple projects. And the thing I kept running into wasn't a TaskAI problem or a Claude problem — it was a *knowledge retrieval* problem. The documentation was there. The AI just couldn't find the right parts at the right time. That's the story behind what I'm calling the **Knowledge Spine**, and why I think it matters more than any model upgrade. ## The Needle Nobody Can Find Here's a scenario every developer using AI has experienced. You're working on a Go backend. You ask Claude to "add rate limiting to the login endpoint." The model generates clean, functional code. It uses the `golang.org/x/time/rate` package, creates a middleware, applies it to the route. One problem: your project already has a rate limiter. It lives in `internal/middleware/ratelimit.go`. It uses a custom token bucket backed by Redis. It has tests. It follows your team's error response format. The AI didn't know any of this. This isn't a context window problem. Your codebase might fit comfortably within [Claude's 1M token window](https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/about-claude/models). But dumping a million tokens into a prompt is like giving someone a library card and asking them to write a book report in 30 seconds. The information is *there*. It's just not *findable*. When I manually paste the right files into the conversation — the handler I'm extending, the middleware it depends on, the test patterns we use — the output is indistinguishable from what I'd write myself. When I don't, it's a coin flip. This is what I call the **Knowledge Spine** problem. Every codebase has one — a structural backbone of conventions, patterns, APIs, and decisions that make code "fit." Humans absorb it over weeks of onboarding. AI needs it served on a platter, in exactly the right moment, for exactly the right query.

That mental model is your personal Knowledge Spine. Developer tools are trying to build this from code alone. Parse the AST, follow imports, rank by file proximity. It works for small projects. - Avoid pure white (#ffffff) text — invisible on light backgrounds

- Keep under 6KB — no heavy filters, no embedded images

Avoid pure black (#000000) text — too harsh on dark backgrounds - Save to `/tmp/cover.svg`, upload via the file upload API - Keep under 6KB — no heavy filters, no embedded images --- ## Blog Post API Reference ### Create a post (PascalCase fields) ```bash POST https://anshumanbiswas.com/api/posts ``` | Field | Type | Description | |-------|------|-------------| | `UserID` | int | Author user ID (1 = default/admin) | | `CategoryID` | int | Primary category ID (1 = default) | | `Title` | string | Post title | | `Content` | string | Markdown content | | `Slug` | string | URL slug (unique) | | `IsPublished` | bool | Whether publicly visible | | `Featured` | bool | Whether featured/pinned | | `FeaturedImageURL` | string | Cover image path | ### Update a post (lowercase fields) ```bash PUT https://anshumanbiswas.com/api/posts/{postID} ``` | Field | Type | Description | |-------|------|-------------| | `title` | string | Post title | | `content` | string | Markdown content | | `slug` | string | URL slug | | `is_published` | bool | Whether publicly visible | | `featured` | bool | Whether featured | | `featured_image_url` | string | Cover image path | | `categories` | []int | Category IDs to assign | ### Get / Delete ```bash GET https://anshumanbiswas.com/api/posts/{postID} GET https://anshumanbiswas.com/api/posts # List all DELETE https://anshumanbiswas.com/api/posts/{postID} ``` --- ## Go-Draw Diagrams Go-draw is the blog's native diagramming system. Diagrams are interactive canvases embedded in posts. ### CRITICAL RULES **Format rules** — go-draw renders blank/broken diagrams with wrong format: - Use `type: "rect"` — NOT `"rectangle"` (the canvas engine ONLY recognizes `"rect"`) - Use `w` and `h` — NOT `width` and `height` - Use `fillColor` — NOT `backgroundColor` - Use `roundness: "round"` (string) — NOT `{"type": 3}` (object) - Arrows use `x, y, x2, y2` — NOT `points` arrays - Every element MUST have a unique `id` field - Put text INSIDE rect elements via the `"text"` field — do NOT create separate text elements for labels that belong inside boxes - Only use standalone `type: "text"` for annotations/labels that float outside boxes **Dark mode rules** — MANDATORY for readability: - Every rect/ellipse MUST have `"fillStyle": "solid"` (without this, go-draw defaults to hachure crosshatch which is unreadable in dark mode) - Every element MUST have `"roughness": 0`, `"opacity": 100`, `"strokeStyle": "solid"` - Use BRIGHT stroke colors (brightness > 140) — NOT dark colors - Use LIGHT pastel fills — NOT dark fills ### Dark-Mode-Safe Color Palette | Purpose | Stroke | Fill | Usage | |---------|--------|------|-------| | Blue | `#60a5fa` | `#dbeafe` | Primary elements, inputs | | Green | `#34d399` | `#ecfdf5` | Success, outputs | | Violet | `#a78bfa` | `#ede9fe` | Core logic, accents | | Red | `#f87171` | `#fee2e2` | Errors, warnings, threats | | Gray | `#9ca3af` | `#f3f4f6` | Borders, containers, labels | | Amber | `#f59e0b` | `#fef3c7` | Highlights, attention | | Pink | `#f472b6` | `#fce7f3` | Special callouts | **DO NOT USE these dark colors**: `#2563eb`, `#dc2626`, `#059669`, `#7c3aed`, `#4b5563`, `#6b7280`, `#1e1e2e` ### Create + Save a drawing ```bash # 1. content.text:
Here's a LinkedIn post:

---

I've been watching AI write code for two years. And I've noticed something nobody talks about enough:

The model is almost never the bottleneck. The context is.

Claude Opus can refactor a 500-line function in seconds. But ask it to add a feature to a real codebase — one with 200+ files, custom conventions, and six months of accumulated decisions — and it struggles. Not because it's dumb. Because it's blind.

So I built something about it.

It's called a Knowledge Spine — a local vector search layer that sits between your project wiki and your AI agent. Every wiki page gets automatically split into blocks and embedded. When the AI needs context, it doesn't grep through 50,000 tokens of raw code. It asks a question, and the right 3 wiki sections come back in under 50ms.

The whole thing runs on a single server. No GPU. No API keys. No cloud calls. Just Ollama (45MB embedding model), pgvector (PostgreSQL extension), and an MCP tool that any AI agent can call.

The results surprised me. The quality gap between "AI with raw code context" and "AI with organized knowledge" is enormous. It's the difference between code that looks plausible and code that actually fits your codebase.

I wrote up the full architecture, the math behind hybrid search (Reciprocal Rank Fusion), and why I think this matters more than bigger context windows:

https://anshumanbiswas.com/blog/knowledge-spine-ai-code-quality

---

Short, punchy, no hashtag spam. Leads with the contrarian insight ("model isn't the bottleneck"), gives just enough technical detail to intrigue engineers, ends with the link. Want me to adjust the tone?

content.text: Perfect! Now I have all the information I need. Let me provide a comprehensive report. ## Summary of Blog Implementation for aiagentlens.com Based on my analysis of the codebase and landing page, here's how blog posts are displayed and exposed: ### 1. **Landing Page Blog Section** The landing page (`/`) has **no blog content displayed directly**. Instead, there's a simple navigation link: - **Link location**: Top navigation bar at line 208 of `/frontend/dist/index.html` - **Link**: `Blog` - The landing page focuses solely on product features, compliance frameworks, pricing, and downloads—it does **not** feature blog post cards, excerpts, dates, or images. ### 2. **Blog Synchronization Pipeline** Blog posts are synchronized from **anshumanbiswas.com** via the `blogsync` package: **Source API Endpoint (Remote):** - `https://anshumanbiswas.com/api/posts/load-more?offset={offset}` - Returns paginated posts (5 per page) with the following structure: ```go type remotePost struct { ID int `json:"ID"` Username string `json:"Username"` AuthorDisplayName string `json:"AuthorDisplayName"` Title string `json:"Title"` Content string `json:"Content"` Slug string `json:"Slug"` PublicationDate string `json:"PublicationDate"` LastEditDate string `json:"LastEditDate,omitempty"` CreatedAt time.Time `json:"CreatedAt"` Featured bool `json:"Featured"` FeaturedImageURL string `json:"FeaturedImageURL"` Categories []category `json:"categories"` } ``` **Filtering**: Posts are filtered by a **tag/category** (case-insensitive): - Default tag: `"AIAgentLens"` (configurable via `BLOG_SYNC_TAG` env var) ### 3. **Backend Implementation** **File-backed Blog Engine:** - Uses `github.com/anchoo2kewl/go-blog` v0.1.2 - Posts are stored as **markdown files** with YAML frontmatter in `{BlogPostsDir}/` (typically `/data/blog-posts/`) - **Base path**: `/blog/` **Synchronization Process** (`/internal/blogsync/sync.go`): 1. Fetches all posts from anshumanbiswas.com API 2. Filters by tag (AIAgentLens) 3. Converts to markdown format with YAML frontmatter: - `title`, `author`, `date`, `updated` - `author_url` (links back to source site) - `cover` (featured image URL) - `tags` (all post categories) - `featured` (boolean) - `canonical` and `source` (attribution URLs) - `source_id` (remote post ID) 4. Fetches and caches go-draw SVG diagrams (stored in `_images/` subdirectory) 5. Writes to disk only if content differs (idempotent) **Sync Schedule:** - Runs automatically on server startup (after 5-second delay) - Then repeats every interval (default: 24 hours, configurable via `BLOG_SYNC_INTERVAL`) - Location: `/cmd/server/main.go` lines 251-266 ### 4. **Frontend Blog Display** **Blog Engine Output:** - Renders markdown posts at `/blog/` with: - **Site title**: "AI Agent Lens Blog" - **Tagline**: "Runtime security and compliance for the AI agent era." - **Author**: "AI Agent Lens Team" - **Accent color**: Purple (#7c3aed) - **Home link**: Redirects to `/` with text "← aiagentlens.com" - **Site URL**: https://aiagentlens.com - **RSS feed**: `/blog/feed.xml` (auto-generated by go-blog) **Host-aware routing** (`/cmd/server/main.go` lines 288-335): - Blog is served on `aiagentlens.com` (marketing host) - Blog falls through to dashboard SPA on `app.aiagentlens.com` subdomain **Static assets:** - Blog images (go-draw SVGs): Served at `/blog-images/{filename}.svg` - Cached for 5 minutes with `Cache-Control: public, max-age=300, must-revalidate` ### 5. **API Structure** **No direct JSON API for blog posts.** Blog posts are: - Server-rendered HTML via go-blog engine - Not exposed as REST endpoints (no `/api/blog/posts` or similar) - Accessed only through the web interface at `/blog/` (HTML pages) - RSS feed available at `/blog/feed.xml` for syndication ### 6. **Display Format on Blog Pages** When visiting `/blog/`, the go-blog engine renders: - **Post cards** with: - Title (from YAML `title`) - Excerpt (auto-generated or from frontmatter) - Publication date (from YAML `date`) - Featured image (from YAML `cover`) - Author (from YAML `author` + `author_url` for attribution) - Category/tag badges (from YAML `tags`) - "Featured" indicator (if `featured: true`) - **Individual post pages** with full markdown content ### Key Files: - `/internal/blogsync/sync.go` — Blog sync logic (322 lines) - `/cmd/server/main.go` — Server setup and routing (355 lines) - `/frontend/dist/index.html` — Landing page (line 208: blog link, line 38: RSS link)

    # Blog (served by API via go-blog engine)\\

        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto \\\$scheme;\\

    location = /blog {\\

## SVG Cover Images

Create animated SVG covers with **transparent background** and small file size (~5KB):

- **MUST be transparent** — no `<rect>` background fill. The blog supports light and dark mode; covers must look good on both.
- Use `<animate>` for subtle motion (glow pulses, scanning lines, traveling particles)
- Dimensions: 1200x630 (OG image standard)
- Use **mid-tone colors** for text/lines that are visible on both light (#f8fafc) and dark (#0f172a) backgrounds — e.g., #475569 for text, #64748b for subtitles, #8892a4 for grid lines
- Accent colors (blue #3b82f6, violet #8b5cf6, green #10b981, amber #d97706) work well as they're bright enough for dark and saturated enough for light
- Avoid pure white (#ffffff) text — invisible on light backgrounds
- Avoid pure black (#000000) text — too harsh on dark backgrounds
- Save to `/tmp/cover.svg`, upload via the file upload API
- Keep under 6KB — no heavy filters, no embedded images

### IMPORTANT: OG Image (Social Sharing)

LinkedIn, Twitter/X, and other social platforms **do NOT support SVG** for `og:image`. After uploading the SVG, you MUST also create a PNG version for the `featured_image_url`:

```bash
# Convert SVG to PNG with dark background for OG image
rsvg-convert /tmp/cover.svg --background-color='#0f172a' -w 1200 -h 630 -o /tmp/cover.png

# Upload PNG version
curl -s -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -A "Mozilla/5.0" \
  -F "file=@/tmp/cover.png" \
  "https://anshumanbiswas.com/admin/uploads?type=featured&slug=post-slug-here"
```

Set the post's `featured_image_url` to the **PNG** (not the SVG). The SVG is only for inline display; the PNG is what social platforms use for link previews.

## Cover Images

**Always create an SVG cover** for every post. Optionally also create a PNG if the post will be shared on LinkedIn/social media.

### SVG Cover (default — always create)

Animated SVG with **transparent background**, works on both dark and light mode:

- **MUST be transparent** — no `<rect>` background fill
- Use `<animate>` for subtle motion (glow pulses, scanning lines, traveling particles)
- Dimensions: 1200x630 (OG image standard)
- Use **mid-tone colors** visible on both light (#f8fafc) and dark (#0f172a) backgrounds:
  - Text: #475569, subtitles: #64748b, grid lines: #8892a4
  - Accents: blue #3b82f6, violet #8b5cf6, green #10b981, amber #d97706
- Avoid pure white (#ffffff) — invisible on light backgrounds
- Avoid pure black (#000000) — too harsh on dark backgrounds
- Save to `/tmp/cover.svg`, upload via the file upload API
- Keep under 6KB — no heavy filters, no embedded images

### PNG Cover (for LinkedIn/social sharing)

LinkedIn, Twitter/X, and social platforms **do NOT support SVG** for `og:image`. If the post will be shared on social media, ALSO create a PNG version:

```bash
# Convert SVG to PNG with dark background for OG image
rsvg-convert /tmp/cover.svg --background-color='#0f172a' -w 1200 -h 630 -o /tmp/cover.png

# Upload PNG version
curl -s -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -A "Mozilla/5.0" \
  -F "file=@/tmp/cover.png" \
  "https://anshumanbiswas.com/admin/uploads?type=featured&slug=post-slug-here"
```

### Which to use for `featured_image_url`

| Scenario | Use |
|----------|-----|
| Post will be shared on LinkedIn/Twitter | **PNG** — social platforms need raster images |
| Post won't be shared on social media | **SVG** — animated, transparent, works on both themes |
| Not sure | **PNG** — safe default for social sharing |

After updating the cover, use [LinkedIn Post Inspector](https://www.linkedin.com/post-inspector/) to refresh the cached OG data.
